new_statements.quote: The Awyu people consider themselves one ethnic group, though they speak a number of closely related languages. [...] The 14th edition of Ethnologue classifies six languages as being Awyu [...]: Awyu Miaro [psa], Awyu Nohon [awj], Siagha-Yenimu [osr], Aghu [ahh], Tsakwambo [kvz], and Jair [yir]. [...] A note on pronunciation: both Awyu and Yaqay have a predominance of stress on the final syllable of a word. Thus place names are pronounced Ketá, Kotúp, Nohón, Bagarám, Wanggaté, Kogó, and Rayám, among others.
new_statements.citation: Kriens, Ronald & Randy Lebold. 2010. Report on the Wildeman River Survey in Papua, Indonesia. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2010-010. Dallas: SIL International.
new_statements.locator: p. 5 (sec. 2 'Background information', 'A note on pronunciation'); scope sentence listing 'Jair [yir]' among the six Awyu languages is on the same page
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (and its, lines 154-173). Every quoted segment is on p.5 (PDF page 5, sec. 2 'Background information') exactly as given; the '[..]' elisions drop only the Ethnologue classification parenthetical and two sentences. 'A note on pronunciation: both Awyu and Yaqay have a predominance of stress on the final syllable of a word. Thus place names are pronounced Ketá, Kotúp, Nohón, Bagarám, Wanggaté, Kogó, and Rayám, among others.' is verbatim. p.26 fn a (Boma II 'Jair' = Jair [yir] > North Awyu [yir]) and table 15 'Awyu V / Jair [yir] / Boma I, Boma II' also verified. WHY I DISAGREE ON READING/STATUS/On the identity of the variety: The reader treats 'Awyu' in the pronunciation note as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey-team impression that Awyu speech (as a group, alongside Yaqay) predominantly stresses the final syllable of the word; evidenced only with place names from the Wildeman-River (Central Awyu and Yaqay) villages, none of them North Awyu.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, impressionistic, from place-name pronunciations; a sociolinguistic survey note, not a phonological analysis, and not specific to the North Awyu (Boma/Kouh) variety. The nearest analysed relative, Aghu (aghu1255, exonym 'Djair/Jair'), is described with a weak accent on the word-final syllable (Drabbe 1957 via van den Heuvel 2016 sec. 1.2.3; de Vries 2020: 10).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's nort2918 'North Awyu' [yir] is the Awyu variety of Boma I ('Auyu Darat'), Boma II ('Jair Auyu') and Kouh on the west bank of the upper Digul (Kouh District, c. 5 deg 48'S 139 deg 52'E), justified solely by Susanto 2004 and Kriens & Lebold 2010:26; it has no grammar, sketch or phonology (Glottolog descriptive refs = 0; OLAC = Susanto 2004 only). Caution on names: ISO yir began as Ethnologue-14 'JAIR' (alt. Djair, Dyair, Yair, Awyu; 1,500 speakers; 'west side of Digul River, south of Kombai, east of Awyu'), a profile that matches Drabbe's 1957 Aghu, whose speakers outsiders called 'Djair' (van den Heuvel 2016:2-5; Wester 2014:6; de Vries 2020:4 'Aghu (Axu, also known as Jair)'). Glottolog files Drabbe 1957 / van den Heuvel 2016 under Aghu [aghu1255], so every published 'Djair/Jair' stress statement (weak accent on the word-final syllable) belongs to aghu1255, not nort2918. The only statement whose stated scope includes yir is Kriens & Lebold's group-level survey remark (final stress in 'Awyu'), evidenced from Central Awyu [cent2118] and Yaqay [yaqa1246] place names.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for nort2918 and the one existing statement (Kriens & Lebold 2010) is 'none found' for this language; this 1931-32 list adds a placement, final stress, for an Awyu variety whose location (between the Digul and Mappi rivers, Mappi settlements) includes the North Awyu villages Boma I/II on the Mapi river, and it is compatible with the Awyu-wide 'predominance of stress on the final syllable' remark in Kriens & Lebold 2010 p. 5 (already held by the project for Central Awyu) and with the Aghu final-stress statements held by the project. It cannot be pinned to North Awyu specifically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is generally on the last syllable. In compounds each constituent word keeps its own stress on what was originally its final syllable, i.e. compounds carry more than one stress rather than a single final one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only via the compound remark: constituent words of compounds retain their (originally final) stress; no explicit secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' -- no exceptions listed. Identity caveat: list 200 is an Awyu wordlist (head chaban ~ Kriens & Lebold 2010 Awyu xaibang/haba, ear soetb ~ suto, tongue fage = fage, tooth maga = maga; not Yaqay muku/mono/inem/manggar), collected 'between the Digul and Mappi rivers' with no north/south limits stated, so it could be North, Central or South Awyu. The same answer-16 wording is given for list 198 Digul Mandobo (p. 150) and list 197 Muyu (pp. 172-173), which are Mandobo and Muyu, not Awyu; the Uwimerah lists 230a-e (pp. 119-132) carry no stress remark.
new_statements.identity_note: Holle list 200 'Digul Mappi' (Stokhof 1982: 133-140) is an Awyu wordlist from 'various settlements in Mappi river area', language area 'between the Digul river and the Mappi river', with the investigator noting possible South, Central and North 'Mappi' dialects; the North Awyu villages Boma I ('Auyu Darat') and Boma II ('Jair Auyu') lie on the Mapi river (Susanto 2004), so North Awyu is inside the stated area, but Central and South Awyu are too; variety unspecified. The Uwimerah (= Wildeman River) lists 230a-e in the same volume, attached by Glottolog to Kokenop Mandobo, have no stress remark. The 'Awya' list 133a in vol. 5/2 (PL D-53) with penult/final stress is a Border-family (Awyi/Taikat) language near Arso, not Awyu. SIL ESR 2012-025 (aerial survey) lists Komyandaret, Korowai, Nakai, Tangko, Tsaukambo, Wambon, Wanggom, not North Awyu.
